extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of logic, philosophy, and scientific method (undergraduates/graduate students and scholars learning principles of deductive reasoning)
extracted.subtask_description: Canonical principles and rules for forming valid deductive inferences (substitution-based treatment of syllogisms, identities, disjunctions) with examples and explanations of common fallacies. Focused on how to produce and judge valid symbolic and ordinary-language deductive arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of equivalents (the one rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: If two terms are stated to be equivalent we may substitute one for the other; this single rule of substitution suffices to reproduce and supersede the elaborate rules of ancient syllogistic logic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly emphasizes that strict observance of substitution of equivalents prevents paralogisms (fallacies). Example guidance: translate negative propositions into affirmative forms and then substitute equivalents. 'So long as we exactly observe the one rule of substitution of equivalents it will be impossible to commit a paralogism.' Use substitution to combine predicates and derive fuller conclusions than older syllogisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference by substituting a definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A term may be replaced by its definition (or vice versa) within propositions to form inferences—definitions permit substituting a long descriptive phrase for a single noun.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'A circle is a curve all points of which are at equal distances from one point' can be used to replace 'circle' by the descriptive phrase. Use substitution to derive equivalent forms; but note: ordinary descriptive lists of predicates are not equivalent to a definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference between a simple and a partial identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Given propositions of the forms A = B and B = BC (partial identity), substitution yields A = BC (substituting B by its equivalent from the other).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Mont Blanc is the highest mountain in Europe (A=B) and Mont Blanc is deeply covered with snow (B=BC). Substitute to infer 'The highest mountain in Europe is deeply covered with snow.' This form is used whenever a term is replaced by its definition or descriptive phrase.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference from two partial identities (Barbara / similar moods)
rubrics_metrics.description: From premises of the forms A = AB and B = BC one may substitute to obtain A = ABC, which in ordinary language yields A has C (e.g., Sodium conducts electricity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit example: (1) Sodium is a metal (A=AB); (2) Metals conduct electricity (B=BC); substitution gives A=ABC, i.e., 'Sodium conducts electricity.' The method covers Barbara and related moods and produces more complete conclusions (including middle-term retention) than traditional syllogisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of a simple identity from two partial identities
rubrics_metrics.description: If A = AB and B = AB (two partial identities sharing the same second member), substitution can yield A = B (a simple identity).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: proving equilateral triangle = equiangular triangle by showing each equals the same composite term. Use this to derive more general/simple identities that capture the information of both premises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inference of a limited identity from two partial identities
rubrics_metrics.description: When premises have the forms B = AB and B = CB, substitution for B in each yields AB = CB, a 'limited identity' relating restricted subclasses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Potassium = potassium metal and Potassium = potassium capable of floating on water, leading to 'Potassium metal = potassium capable of floating on water.' The method gives a more exact conclusion than classical syllogisms such as Darapti.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ellipsis of terms / Intrinsic minimization
rubrics_metrics.description: You may drop any term appearing in one member of a proposition provided you substitute for it the whole of the other member—this allows omission of needless terms by substitutive reasoning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Called 'Intrinsic Minimization' or 'Ellipsis of Terms': e.g., from A = ABC one can derive A = AC by repeated substitution and coalescence of repeated letters (using the Law of Simplicity). Use this to abridge composite conclusions into the ordinary elliptical form used in common language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sorites / chain substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: A chain of propositions allowing repeated substitution (a sorites) can be combined stepwise to produce a single composite conclusion that carries all predicates across the chain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example chain: Iron is a metal; metals are good conductors; good conductors are useful for telegraphy — yields 'Iron is useful for telegraphic purposes.' Formally substitute successive equivalents to reach A = ABCD.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining varied-form premises by substitution
rubrics_metrics.description: Premises of mixed character (identities, partial identities, negative terms) can still be combined by substitution into a precise composite conclusion when the symbolic combinations permit substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Common salt is sodium chloride', 'sodium chloride crystallizes cubically', and 'things crystallizing cubically do not double-refract' combine to 'Common salt does not double-refract.' Convert each premise to the A = ... form and substitute successively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of ordinary description vs definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A long list of predicates combined by substitution yields a descriptive composite but is not equivalent to a strict definition of a substance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: listing copper's many properties and combining them into A = ABC...K gives a full description but not a definition; no amount of ordinary description is strictly equivalent to a definition of a substance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two negative premises usually give no conclusion (with qualification)
rubrics_metrics.description: When both premises are negative there is generally no substitutional relation enabling a conclusion, aligning with the syllogistic rule that two negative premises yield no conclusion—however, exceptions occur when negatives can be converted to affirmatives enabling substitution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Granite is not a sedimentary rock' and 'Basalt is not a sedimentary rock' give no relation between granite and basalt because no common term is presented in compatible form. But 'Whatever is not metallic is not capable of magnetic influence' plus 'Carbon is not metallic' can be translated to affirmative equivalents and yield a valid negative conclusion by substitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding fallacy of the Undistributed Middle
rubrics_metrics.description: If the middle term is undistributed (combined differently in the two premises) substitution cannot produce a relation between the extremes, so no valid conclusion follows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Hydrogen is an element' and 'All metals are elements' translate to A = AB and C = CB; because B appears differently no substitution is possible—this is the classical undistributed middle fallacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illicit Process of the Major Term (and related illicit substitutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: One must not substitute a wider term for a narrower one (or otherwise substitute for a term something not shown equivalent); illicit substitution produces fallacious conclusions like asserting a non-relation between B and C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example (illustrating impossibility): from 'All planets are subject to gravity' and 'Fixed stars are not planets' one cannot legitimately infer 'Fixed stars are not subject to gravity' because no valid substitution connects fixed stars to the gravity term. The substitution rule prevents such illicit processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fallacy of Four Terms and Illicit Minor Term (general prohibition)
rubrics_metrics.description: When two propositions contain four distinct terms or when one substitutes a term for a wider unknown equivalent, substitution cannot be performed and no conclusion is justified.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If premises are A = B and C = D (four distinct terms) then no substitution opens; illicit minor term consists in substituting a term by another wider term not shown equivalent—both are prevented by strict substitution practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of disjunctive propositions (alternative relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disjunctive propositions list alternatives joined by 'or' and express the inverse process of generalization; the author introduces a special symbol (.|.) to represent the alternative relation instead of +.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use .|. to represent alternatives because mathematical addition (+) suggests an analogy that is imperfect. Represent disjunctions like 'A planet is either Mercury .|. Venus .|. Earth .|. ...' and treat the alternatives formally when combining with other propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature of disjunctive/alternative relation (ignorance/doubt/choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: The disjunctive (alternative) relation expresses ignorance/doubt about which specific subclass an object belongs to and so gives rise to choice; disjunction undoes generalization by distinguishing constituent parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a general term is used (e.g., 'planet' or 'vertebrate animal') a disjunctive proposition enumerates the possible constituent species and thereby resolves uncertainty. Use disjunctions to specify subordinate classes and be careful about the intended exclusivity of alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusive vs. unexclusive (compossible) alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether alternatives in a disjunction are exclusive (cannot be true together) or unexclusive/compossible (may be true together); this materially affects interpretation and inference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Arches are circular or pointed' (exclusive) vs 'Luminous bodies are self-luminous or luminous by reflection' (possibly compossible). Historical debate exists; sometimes exclusivity is implicit via tacit premises. Choose exclusive alternatives when possible for clarity, but recognize many ordinary-language disjunctions are not exclusive.
